content.title: Moya Brennan obituary: ‘first lady of Celtic music’
content.text: video Grammy-winning singer, harpist and founder member of Clannad dies aged 73 Moya Brennan and the rest of Clannad, from left to right, Pádraig Duggan, Ciarán Brennan, Noel Duggan and Pól Brennan John Rodgers/Redferns Tuesday April 14 2026, 5.00pm BST, The Times Growing up in a tiny village in Co Donegal on Ireland’s wild Atlantic coast, Moya Brennan always knew she was born to sing. Her mother was a music teacher and her father was a member of a show band with whom she performed as a child. More importantly, though, her parents owned the local pub Leo’s Tavern, or Tabhairne Leo as it is better known in Donegal, and where, in the great Irish tradition, music was as much a part of the craic as the drinking. During the nightly sessions in the backroom of the tavern the teenage Brennan learnt the traditional Gaelic songs that were to become her passport to fame. What she never imagined was that the family band of sisters, brothers and uncles known as Clannad that emerged from those informal pub sessions would go on to sell 15 million records and that she would end up singing in Gaelic on Top of the Pops, the first act ever to do so. The hit song that launched an obscure traditional folk band to global success was titled Theme from Harry’s Game and was written by Brennan and her brothers Ciarán and Pól for ITV’s 1982 drama about the Troubles. Featuring Brennan’s ethereal voice over lush synthesisers and layered harmonies, the song reached No 5 in the UK singles chart, despite briefly being banned after a false claim that the Irish lyrics expressed support for the IRA. In fact, Brennan had glossed the words from a book of ancient Irish proverbs and the lyric translated roughly as “Everything that is and will be, will cease to be, the moon and the stars, youth and beauty.” “Clannad were never a political band,” she insisted, and what she liked about Harry’s Game was the drama’s message that “nobody wins in war”. The song’s success took everyone by surprise. “One day, we were in a Transit van in Germany; the next we were being picked up in a limo to do Top of the Pops,” Brennan recalled. The gold disc for the recording, along with numerous others, has for the past four decades hung above the bar in Leo’s Tavern, which remains in the family under the proprietorship of Brennan’s brother Bartley. For a long time U2 used the theme as a warm-up before taking the stage, and Bono subsequently duetted with Brennan on Clannad’s 1985 hit In a Lifetime. He praised her for possessing “one of the greatest voices the human ear has ever experienced” and claimed that when he first heard Theme from Harry’s Game, on his car radio, he had to pull over because the song reduced him to tears. For many years Brennan and Clannad resisted record company pressure to sing in English but eventually did so when they were commissioned to score the ITV drama series Robin of Sherwood, which ran over 26 episodes between 1984 and 1986. The soundtrack album made the UK Top 20 and led to an 18-month world tour that took them to America and the Soviet Union. Brennan was a skilled harpist C Brandon/Redferns via Getty Images By then the old Donegal folk songs were being replaced in the group’s repertoire by a hybrid style that fused Celtic influences with a glossy pop sensibility that won them Grammy award nominations for best new age album on three occasions. Although Clannad did not score the film Titanic, the American composer James Horner who did admitted his soundtrack was heavily indebted to the spirit of the group’s romantic mix of swirling Celtic mists and mellifluous pop modernity, and Brennan sang the 1910 song Come Josephine in My Flying Machine over the scene in which Kate Winslet’s character, Rose, floats in the Atlantic. Brennan became known as the “first lady of Celtic music” but success took its toll. In her 2000 autobiography The Other Side of the Rainbow she wrote candidly of her “dark years” in which she struggled with drug and alcohol abuse and a chaotic personal life. She was also open about the toll that travelling to England for an abortion in 1972 had taken on her. Her first marriage to the Dublin musician Pat Farrell in the mid-1980s collapsed, she suffered a miscarriage and was briefly in a relationship with U2’s bassist Adam Clayton. “The same big party went on night after night,” she recalled. “You’d wake up and say, ‘I’m never doing that again’. But, the next night, you’d be in another party and it was easy to get on that rollercoaster of excess. I really lost myself.” Salvation came when she rediscovered her faith and met Tim Jarvis, a photographer who visited Donegal to take pictures of the band for the NME. They married in 1990 and he survives her along with their children, Aisling and Paul Jarvis, who co-produced and played on her 2017 solo album Canvas. In Oslo in 2022 Per Ole Hagen/Redferns She is further survived by her brothers and fellow Clannad members Ciarán and Pól Brennan and by her sister Enya, who briefly sung with the group in the early 1980s before becoming a chart-topping solo star. Her uncles Pádraig Duggan and Noel Duggan, who were twin brothers and founder members of the group, died in 2016 and 2022 respectively. In 2009 she changed her legal name to Moya Brennan by deed poll but she was born Máire Philomena Ní Bhraonáin in 1952 in Dublin, the eldest of nine children to Máire (née Ní Dhúgáin), known as Baba, and Leo Brennan. Growing up in the remote parish of Gweedore (Gaoth Dobhair), Co Donegal, speaking Irish as her first language, she was 15 when her parents took over a dilapidated bar in nearby Meenaleck. As Leo’s Tavern, they turned it into the hub of the local community, hosting live music every night with family members at the heart of the sessions. In 1970 the family group won a competition at the annual Letterkenny Folk Festival — with a recording contract with Philips as the prize. At the time they called themselves Clann as Dobhar (Irish for “Family from Dore”) but shortened the name to Clannad in 1973 when their debut album was released. The label wanted them to sing in English so they switched to Gael Linn, a record company which specialised in traditional Irish music, before they found international success with RCA. The first of several solo albums under the name Máire Brennan appeared in 1992 and she adopted the spelling Moya a decade later. Away from Clannad she duetted with Shane MacGowan, Robert Plant, Bruce Hornsby and Ronan Keating among others while the group went on a decade-long hiatus. At the Royal Opera House, LondonJames Emmett/Redferns The group reunited after a family birthday party at the pub in Donegal in 2007. Their final album Nadur appeared in 2013, before both the death of Pádraig and Moya’s illness with pulmonary fibrosis (she faced the prospect of a double lung transplant) seemed to have ended the story. However in 2020, on the 50th anniversary of the group’s formation, they commenced a farewell tour under the title In a Lifetime. After a handful of dates, it was put on hold by the pandemic and the tour did not conclude until 2023. Yet it was not quite the end. Fittingly the final chapter of the story took place where it had all started when last year Brennan and the other surviving band members came together for an intimate concert at Leo’s Tavern in aid of a Donegal cancer charity. A philanthropist, Brennan also worked with Christian Blind Mission Ireland, for which she travelled widely in Africa and South America, and there were numerous benefit concerts, including an event in Rome for Pope John Paul II and another in Cologne with Pope Benedict XVI — both of which she regarded as highlights of her career. Brennan in Finsbury Park, north London, in 2011Shutterstock Editorial “I start every day with prayer. I’d be very lost without a sense of knowing that I’m not alone,” she said. “I feel I can take on anything when God is part of my life.” Moya Brennan, singer and harpist, was born on August 4, 1952. She died after a short illness on April 13, 2026, aged 73
